frameworks.name: Expert Mapping and Consolidation Method
frameworks.definition: A rapid learning framework that identifies the smartest people around a problem, maps the neural network of expertise by iterative referral, and consolidates knowledge into actionable buckets.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi learned rapid skill acquisition as a 22-year-old management consultant working on defense department projects (space, cyber, intelligence focus). The method: identify five smartest people around a problem, ask each for five referrals, iterate until names repeat, then consolidate their knowledge into buckets, recode, distill, and create a presentation. This expert-mapping approach became his framework for learning any new endeavor.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Mapping the neural network of expertise through iterative referral identification, then consolidating dispersed knowledge into organized buckets reduces the time-to-insight by creating an exhaustive expert atlas instead of consulting individual experts serially.

claims.text: Hormozi evaluates entry into any new industry using a first-pass filter: difficulty (easier or harder than expected) and fit (problems that arise + own ability to solve). Industries with novel, solvable problems rank higher than those with well-known constraints.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Industries present unknown-unknowns and known-unknowns; the filtering question is whether the problems align with personal capability, not whether the industry is easy.

claims.text: Insurance presents an interesting entry opportunity for Hormozi because the core constraint is customer acquisition (demand-driven, not capital-constrained), it has high retention (people need it), premium tax advantages, and regulatory barriers create moat—but people dislike it, making acquisition hard. The magic entry point will emerge only after discovering a specific, defensible acquisition angle not yet visible.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
bounded_by: Does not apply to capital-constrained insurance segments
Does not apply unless acquisition, not product quality, is the binding constraint

claims.text: Hormozi approaches all new industries with the consultant's perspective: ask yourself first whether you are willing to spend deep time learning it, then do the expert-mapping research. The willingness filter precedes the competence-building investment.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

examples.text: At 22 years old, Hormozi worked on defense department projects after obtaining a top-secret security clearance. The projects focused on space, cyber, and intelligence, and involved determining optimal asset allocation to achieve military objectives. He had four months to prepare a presentation worth four million dollars for a project that would be presented to two three-star generals and one four-star general with decades of experience. To prepare, Hormozi interviewed five of the smartest people around the problem, asked each for five referrals, and iterated this process until the same names repeated. He consolidated their knowledge into organized buckets, recoded the insights, distilled them down, and created a presentation—this entire process was the core consulting method.

Hormozi evaluated insurance as a potential business opportunity. Insurance is a high-retention business (people need coverage) with regulatory moats and superior tax structures. The binding constraint is not capital availability (which is abundant) but customer acquisition—the product is essential but unpopular, making it difficult to acquire customers. Hormozi identified this constraint but noted that the actual winning angle inside insurance has not yet emerged; it will require deeper exploration to find the specific defensible edge.

practices.text: When evaluating a new industry, first ask yourself: do I actually want to spend deep time learning this? Only proceed with the expert-mapping research if the answer is yes.

To rapidly become expert in a field, identify five smart people around the problem, interview each, ask them for five referrals to other smart people, and iterate until names repeat. Then consolidate and distill the knowledge into a presentation.
